subject: Physics
title: Atoms
summary: How the alpha-particle scattering experiment forced the nuclear model of the atom, why that model could not be stable under classical physics, and how Bohr's three postulates give the radius, speed and energy of the electron in hydrogen and explain its line spectrum. It opens Unit VIII (Atoms and Nuclei) and the Bohr derivation, the energy-level diagram and the spectral-series numericals are among the most predictable questions in the paper.

exam_profile.weightage: Unit VIII (Atoms and Nuclei: Chapters 12 and 13) carries 7 marks in the CBSE Class 12 Physics paper. Atoms typically takes 3 to 4 of those: one 3-mark or 5-mark question built around Bohr's model (derivation of r<sub>n</sub>, v<sub>n</sub> or E<sub>n</sub>, or a transition numerical), plus a 1-mark MCQ or assertion-reason on scattering, energy levels or spectral series.

question_types.note: How r<sub>n</sub>, v<sub>n</sub>, E<sub>n</sub> and the orbital period scale with n; the value of energy or angular momentum in a given orbit; which series lies in the visible or ultraviolet; number of spectral lines from level n; what the distance of closest approach depends on; why gold and why alpha-particles were used.

Negative total energy meaning a bound electron; electrons in stationary orbits not radiating; most alpha-particles passing undeflected because the atom is mostly empty; Bohr's model failing for multi-electron atoms; the Balmer series being in the visible region.

State two Bohr postulates; define distance of closest approach or impact parameter; write the expression for r<sub>n</sub> or E<sub>n</sub> and find a value; a one-step transition numerical; the trajectory of alpha-particles for different impact parameters; the ratio of two wavelengths in a series.

Derive the radius of the nth orbit from Bohr's postulates; explain the second postulate using de Broglie's hypothesis with a diagram; a numerical on a 12.5 eV electron beam or a photon exciting hydrogen and the lines emitted; the Geiger-Marsden observations and the conclusions drawn from each; energy-level diagram with the series marked.

Using Bohr's postulates derive r<sub>n</sub>, v<sub>n</sub> and the total energy E<sub>n</sub>, then obtain the Rydberg formula and explain the hydrogen spectrum with an energy-level diagram; or describe the alpha-scattering experiment, its findings and Rutherford's model with its limitations, then state how Bohr removed them.

A passage on the Geiger-Marsden experiment or on Bohr's model and hydrogen spectrum followed by four one-mark parts, usually two conceptual and two short numericals (closest approach, energy of a level, wavelength of a line).

hot_topics: Bohr's postulates and the derivation of r<sub>n</sub>, v<sub>n</sub> and E<sub>n</sub> for hydrogen
Energy-level diagram of hydrogen and the spectral series (Lyman, Balmer, Paschen)
Transition numericals: energy, wavelength and frequency of emitted or absorbed photons
Alpha-particle scattering experiment: observations, conclusions and the nuclear model
Distance of closest approach and impact parameter
de Broglie's explanation of Bohr's second postulate
Limitations of Rutherford's model and of Bohr's model
Kinetic, potential and total energy of the orbiting electron and their signs

sections.heading: 12.1 Introduction
sections.body:
By 1897 J. J. Thomson had shown that every atom contains negatively charged electrons that are far lighter than the atom itself. Since atoms are electrically neutral, they must also contain an equal amount of positive charge, and this positive part must carry almost all the mass. The question the chapter answers is how the positive charge and the electrons are arranged inside the atom.

Thomson's first guess, the plum-pudding model (1898), spreads the positive charge uniformly over the whole atom and embeds the electrons in it like seeds in a watermelon. It explains neutrality but, as you will see, cannot survive the alpha-scattering experiment.

The other clue was atomic spectra. A gas excited in a discharge tube does not emit a continuous rainbow. It emits only a set of sharp, bright lines at definite wavelengths, and each element has its own set of lines, a fingerprint. Any correct atomic model must explain why the emitted radiation comes only at those particular wavelengths. Rutherford's nuclear model, built from the scattering experiment, explains the structure but not the spectrum and not the stability. Bohr's model, built on top of Rutherford's, explains all three for hydrogen. That progression, Thomson to Rutherford to Bohr, is the spine of the chapter, and the examiner expects you to know what each model got right and what forced the next one.
sections.tip: One-mark questions like to ask what Thomson's model explained (neutrality, electrons as constituents) and what it could not (large-angle alpha scattering, line spectra). Keep both lists ready.

sections.heading: 12.2 Alpha-particle Scattering and Rutherford's Nuclear Model of Atom
sections.body:
In 1911, at Rutherford's suggestion, Geiger and Marsden fired alpha-particles from a radioactive source (21483Bi) at a thin gold foil about 2.1 × 10−7 m thick. The beam was collimated by a lead-brick slit, and the scattered alpha-particles were counted by the flashes they produced on a zinc sulphide screen viewed through a microscope. The alpha-particles had kinetic energy 5.5 MeV. Gold was chosen because it is very malleable, so an extremely thin foil could be made, and because the gold nucleus is heavy, so it does not recoil and the scattering is clean.

Observations and what each one means, which is exactly how the marking scheme wants it:

  • Most alpha-particles passed straight through with little or no deflection. So most of the atom is empty space.
  • Only about 0.14% were scattered by more than 1°, and about 1 in 8000 was deflected by more than 90°, some almost straight back. A 5.5 MeV alpha-particle can only be turned back by a very strong repulsive force, so the entire positive charge and almost all the mass of the atom must be concentrated in a tiny region, the nucleus. The plum-pudding model, with its spread-out charge, cannot produce such a force.

Rutherford's nuclear model: the atom has a small, dense, positively charged nucleus of size about 10−15 m to 10−14 m, while the atom is about 10−10 m across, so the nucleus is roughly 104 times smaller. Electrons revolve around the nucleus in orbits, held by the Coulomb attraction, the way planets are held by gravity. The electrons and the nucleus together make the atom neutral.

The alpha-particle experiences only the Coulomb repulsion of the gold nucleus, F = (1/4πε0) · (2e)(Ze)/r2, with Z = 79 for gold. Since the nucleus is about fifty times heavier than the alpha-particle it stays at rest, and the electrons are far too light to deflect the alpha-particle appreciably. Rutherford calculated the number of alpha-particles scattered at each angle from this force law, and Geiger and Marsden's counts matched, which confirmed the model.

where: Coulomb repulsion between alpha-particle (charge 2e) and nucleus (charge Ze)
distance between the alpha-particle and the nucleus (m)
atomic number of the target, 79 for gold

sections.tip: If asked why alpha-particles and not electrons or protons: alpha-particles are heavy and doubly charged, so they are not deflected by the atomic electrons and give a clear, measurable scattering pattern from the nucleus alone.

sections.heading: 12.2.1 Alpha-particle trajectory
sections.body:
The path of an alpha-particle is fixed by its impact parameter b, the perpendicular distance between the initial velocity vector of the alpha-particle and the centre of the nucleus. A particle with large b passes far from the nucleus, feels a weak force and is barely deflected. As b decreases, the deflection grows. For a head-on approach, b = 0, the particle comes to rest momentarily and is scattered back through 180°. Because the nucleus is so small, only a tiny fraction of the alpha-particles have small enough b to suffer large-angle scattering, which is why large deflections are rare. The relation between b and the scattering angle θ, which NCERT states but does not derive, is b = (Ze2 cot(θ/2))/(4πε0 · ½mv2).

Distance of closest approach (derive this, it is a regular 2- or 3-marker). For the head-on case the alpha-particle of kinetic energy K stops at a distance d from the nucleus where all its kinetic energy has become electrostatic potential energy:

K = (1/4πε0) · (2e)(Ze)/d, so d = 2Ze2/(4πε0K).

For a 7.7 MeV alpha-particle on gold (NCERT Example 12.1): K = 7.7 × 1.6 × 10−13 J = 1.23 × 10−12 J, and d = (9 × 109)(2 × 79)(1.6 × 10−19)2/(1.23 × 10−12) = 3.64 × 10−26/1.23 × 10−12 ≈ 3.0 × 10−14 m = 30 fm. This is an upper limit on the size of the gold nucleus; the actual radius is about 6 fm, so the alpha-particle never touches the nucleus and the pure Coulomb calculation is valid.

Two things the examiner looks for: d ∝ 1/K, so doubling the kinetic energy halves the distance of closest approach; and d ∝ Z, so a heavier nucleus turns the particle back sooner.

where: distance of closest approach for a head-on collision (m)
initial kinetic energy of the alpha-particle (J)
atomic number of the target nucleus

sections.tip: Convert MeV to joule (1 MeV = 1.6 × 10<sup>−13</sup> J) before substituting, and remember the alpha-particle charge is 2e, not e. Both slips are common and both cost the final mark.

sections.heading: 12.2.2 Electron orbits
sections.body:
In Rutherford's picture the electron moves in a circular orbit of radius r around the nucleus, with the Coulomb attraction supplying the centripetal force. For hydrogen (Z = 1):

mv2/r = (1/4πε0) · e2/r2, so r = e2/(4πε0 m v2).

From the same equation the kinetic energy is K = ½mv2 = e2/(8πε0r). The potential energy of the electron at distance r from the proton is U = −e2/(4πε0r), negative because the force is attractive. So the total energy is

E = K + U = e2/(8πε0r) − e2/(4πε0r) = −e2/(8πε0r).

Three relations you should be able to quote at once: K = −E, U = 2E, and U = −2K. The total energy is negative, which means the electron is bound to the nucleus; energy equal to |E| must be supplied to free it. If E were positive the electron would escape and there would be no atom.

Now the fatal problem, which is the standard answer to "state the limitations of Rutherford's model":

  • An electron in a circular orbit is accelerated, and classical electromagnetic theory says an accelerated charge radiates. The electron would lose energy continuously, its orbit would shrink, and it would spiral into the nucleus in about 10−8 s. The atom would collapse. Real atoms are stable.
  • As the electron spiralled in, its frequency of revolution would change continuously, so the radiation emitted would have a continuous spread of frequencies. But atoms emit line spectra, with only certain discrete frequencies.

Rutherford's model gives the structure but has no answer to either objection. That is where Bohr comes in.

where: total energy, negative for a bound electron (J)

sections.tip: "Significance of negative total energy" is a favourite 1- or 2-mark part: it means the electron is bound to the nucleus and cannot leave unless it is given energy equal to |E|.

sections.heading: 12.3 Atomic Spectra
sections.body:
When a gas or vapour is excited at low pressure by passing an electric current, it emits radiation. Passed through a prism or grating, this radiation shows a set of bright lines on a dark background, an emission line spectrum. The pattern of wavelengths is characteristic of the element, so a spectrum identifies the element the way a fingerprint identifies a person. Conversely, if white light is passed through the same cool gas, dark lines appear in the continuous spectrum at exactly the wavelengths the gas would emit; this is the absorption spectrum.

Hydrogen, the simplest atom, has the simplest spectrum. In 1885 Balmer found that the visible lines of hydrogen, Hα at 656.3 nm (red), Hβ at 486.1 nm (blue-green), Hγ at 434.1 nm (violet) and Hδ at 410.2 nm (violet), fit a single empirical formula:

1/λ = R (1/22 − 1/n2), n = 3, 4, 5, ...

with R, the Rydberg constant, equal to 1.097 × 107 m−1. Putting n = 3 gives 656.3 nm, n = 4 gives 486.1 nm and so on. As n increases, the lines crowd closer together and become fainter, converging to the series limit at n → ∞, where 1/λ = R/4 and λ = 364.6 nm.

Other series were found later in the ultraviolet and infrared and are named after their discoverers. Rydberg generalised Balmer's formula to 1/λ = R (1/nf2 − 1/ni2) with ni > nf. These were empirical fits with no physical reason behind them. Explaining where this formula comes from, and why R has the value it has, is the test that Bohr's model passes and Rutherford's fails.
sections.tip: A quick check for Balmer numericals: the first line is 656 nm and the series limit is 365 nm. Any Balmer wavelength you calculate must lie between the two.

sections.heading: 12.4 Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom
sections.body:
In 1913 Niels Bohr kept Rutherford's nucleus and orbiting electron but added three postulates that classical physics does not permit. Write them exactly like this in the exam.

  1. Stationary orbits. An electron in an atom can revolve only in certain stable orbits without emitting radiation, even though it is accelerating. Each such orbit has a definite total energy; these are the stationary states of the atom.
  2. Quantisation of angular momentum. The electron revolves only in those orbits for which its angular momentum is an integral multiple of h/2π: L = mvr = nh/2π, n = 1, 2, 3, ... This picks out the allowed orbits from the continuum that Rutherford's model permits.
  3. Frequency condition. An electron may jump from a higher-energy orbit to a lower one; when it does, a photon is emitted whose energy equals the energy difference of the two states: hν = Ei − Ef. (Absorption of a photon of the same energy causes the reverse jump.)

Derivation of rn and vn (the 3-marker). From the Coulomb force as centripetal force, mv2/r = e2/(4πε0r2) ... (1). From the second postulate, mvr = nh/2π ... (2). Divide (1) by (2)2 after squaring (2): from (2), v = nh/(2πmr); substitute in (1): m n2h2/(4π2m2r3) = e2/(4πε0r2), giving

rn = (n2/m) (h/2π)2 (4πε0/e2) = n2 ε0h2/(π m e2).

Then from (2), vn = nh/(2πmrn) = (1/n) (e2/4πε0) (1/(h/2π)) = e2/(2ε0nh).

So rn ∝ n2 and vn ∝ 1/n. For n = 1, r1 = 5.29 × 10−11 m, the Bohr radius a0, which matches the known size of the hydrogen atom; and v1 = 2.18 × 106 m s−1, about c/137. The number v1/c = e2/(2ε0hc) ≈ 1/137 is the fine-structure constant α; its smallness justifies the non-relativistic treatment. The orbital period Tn = 2πrn/vn ∝ n3, with T1 = 1.53 × 10−16 s.

where: angular momentum of the electron (kg m<sup>2</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>)

formulas.expr: r<sub>n</sub> = n<sup>2</sup> ε<sub>0</sub>h<sup>2</sup>/(π m e<sup>2</sup>) = n<sup>2</sup> a<sub>0</sub>, a<sub>0</sub> = 5.29 × 10<sup>−11</sup> m
where: Bohr radius, radius of the ground-state orbit

formulas.expr: v<sub>n</sub> = e<sup>2</sup>/(2ε<sub>0</sub>nh) = v<sub>1</sub>/n, v<sub>1</sub> = 2.18 × 10<sup>6</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>
where: speed of the electron in the nth orbit (m s<sup>−1</sup>)
energies of the initial and final stationary states (J)

sections.tip: For a hydrogen-like ion of atomic number Z replace e<sup>2</sup> by Ze<sup>2</sup>: r<sub>n</sub> = n<sup>2</sup>a<sub>0</sub>/Z, v<sub>n</sub> = Zv<sub>1</sub>/n, E<sub>n</sub> = −13.6 Z<sup>2</sup>/n<sup>2</sup> eV. He<sup>+</sup> (Z = 2) and Li<sup>2+</sup> (Z = 3) MCQs use exactly this.

sections.heading: 12.4.1 Energy levels
sections.body:
Derivation of En (the 5-marker, continued from the radius). Kinetic energy Kn = ½mvn2 = e2/(8πε0rn) and potential energy Un = −e2/(4πε0rn), so the total energy is En = −e2/(8πε0rn). Substituting rn = n2ε0h2/(πme2):

En = −me4/(8 n2 ε02 h2).

Putting in the constants, En = −2.18 × 10−18/n2 J = −13.6/n2 eV. The energy is negative in every orbit, so the electron is bound. En ∝ −1/n2: it rises towards zero as n increases, and the levels get closer and closer together. At n → ∞ the energy is zero and the electron is free.

The lowest state n = 1 is the ground state, with E1 = −13.6 eV. Higher states are excited states: E2 = −3.40 eV, E3 = −1.51 eV, E4 = −0.85 eV, E5 = −0.54 eV. Memorise these five; almost every transition numerical uses them. The minimum energy needed to free the electron from the ground state is the ionisation energy, 13.6 eV, which agrees with experiment and was one of Bohr's great successes. The energy needed to take the atom from the ground state to the first excited state, 13.6 − 3.4 = 10.2 eV, is the first excitation energy. The ionisation potential is 13.6 V and the first excitation potential is 10.2 V.

The energy-level diagram (Fig. 12.4 in NCERT) is drawn as horizontal lines, n = 1 at the bottom labelled −13.6 eV, n = 2 above it at −3.4 eV, and so on, with n = ∞ at 0 eV at the top. The spacing shrinks rapidly upward. At room temperature almost all hydrogen atoms sit in the ground state; they must be excited by a collision or a photon before they can emit.

In every state Kn = −En = 13.6/n2 eV and Un = 2En = −27.2/n2 eV. In the ground state, K = 13.6 eV and U = −27.2 eV, which is NCERT Exercise 12.4 and a routine 2-mark question.

where: total energy of the electron in the nth orbit
permittivity of free space, 8.85 × 10<sup>−12</sup> C<sup>2</sup> N<sup>−1</sup> m<sup>−2</sup>
kinetic energy in the nth orbit
potential energy in the nth orbit

sections.tip: Ionisation energy of hydrogen from the level n is 13.6/n<sup>2</sup> eV, so from the first excited state it is only 3.4 eV. Read whether the question starts from the ground state or an excited one.

sections.heading: 12.5 The Line Spectra of the Hydrogen Atom
sections.body:
Bohr's third postulate turns the energy levels into a spectrum. For a jump from a higher level ni to a lower level nf, the photon energy is hν = Ei − Ef = (me4/(8ε02h2)) (1/nf2 − 1/ni2). With ν = c/λ,

1/λ = (me4/(8ε02h3c)) (1/nf2 − 1/ni2) = R (1/nf2 − 1/ni2).

This is exactly Rydberg's empirical formula, and the theory now predicts the constant: R = me4/(8ε02h3c), which NCERT evaluates as 1.03 × 107 m−1, close to the measured 1.097 × 107 m−1. Explaining Balmer's formula from first principles is the strongest evidence for Bohr's model. Use R = 1.097 × 107 m−1 in numericals, or the shortcut E (in eV) = 1240/λ (in nm).

Each series is a set of transitions ending on the same lower level:

  • Lyman series: nf = 1, ni = 2, 3, 4, ...; ultraviolet. First line 121.6 nm, series limit 91.2 nm.
  • Balmer series: nf = 2, ni = 3, 4, ...; visible (and near UV). First line Hα 656.3 nm, limit 364.6 nm.
  • Paschen series: nf = 3; infrared. First line 1875 nm.
  • Brackett series: nf = 4; infrared.
  • Pfund series: nf = 5; infrared.

The first line of a series (smallest ni) has the longest wavelength; the series limit (ni → ∞) has the shortest wavelength, λmin = nf2/R. The number of possible lines when atoms are excited to level n and then de-excite by every route is n(n − 1)/2: six lines from n = 4, three from n = 3.

Absorption works the same way in reverse: a ground-state atom absorbs a photon only if its energy equals En − E1 for some n. A photon of 12.75 eV lifts it to n = 4; a photon of 12.5 eV, which matches no level, is not absorbed at all.

Limitations of Bohr's model (learn two): it applies only to hydrogen and hydrogen-like one-electron ions, not to atoms with more than one electron, because it ignores electron-electron interactions; and it gives the frequencies of the lines but says nothing about their relative intensities, nor about fine structure, nor about the splitting of lines in magnetic fields.

where: lower (final) level: 1 Lyman, 2 Balmer, 3 Paschen, 4 Brackett, 5 Pfund
wavelength in nanometre; hc = 1240 eV nm

sections.tip: Name the series from n<sub>f</sub> only. A transition n = 5 to n = 2 is Balmer, whatever the starting level. And the shortest wavelength in a series comes from n<sub>i</sub> = ∞, not from the second line.

sections.heading: 12.6 de Broglie's Explanation of Bohr's Second Postulate of Quantisation
sections.body:
Bohr could not say why angular momentum should come only in multiples of h/2π. In 1923 de Broglie supplied the reason: the electron is a wave as well as a particle, with wavelength λ = h/mv, and an orbit is allowed only if the electron wave fits into it as a standing wave.

Think of a string fixed at both ends. It vibrates only in modes where a whole number of half-wavelengths fit the length. For a wave running round a closed loop the condition is that a whole number of wavelengths fit the circumference; otherwise the wave interferes destructively with itself after each round and dies out. So for the nth orbit,

2πrn = nλ, n = 1, 2, 3, ...

Substituting λ = h/mvn: 2πrn = nh/(mvn), which rearranges to mvnrn = nh/2π. That is Bohr's second postulate exactly. Quantisation of angular momentum is nothing more than the statement that the electron's matter wave must be a standing wave around the orbit.

The diagram the examiner wants: a circle for the orbit with a wavy line drawn around it that closes on itself after exactly n wavelengths (draw n = 4 or so, the standing-wave pattern with crests and troughs alternating around the circle). Label 2πr = nλ.

Two more points that fetch marks. First, the electron speed in the ground state, 2.18 × 106 m s−1, gives λ = h/mv = 6.63 × 10−34/(9.1 × 10−31 × 2.18 × 106) = 3.3 × 10−10 m, which is exactly the circumference 2π × 5.29 × 10−11 m of the first orbit, as it should be for n = 1. Second, the de Broglie picture removes the arbitrariness but not the other limitations of the Bohr model; a full treatment needs quantum mechanics, where the electron has no definite orbit at all, only a probability distribution.

where: de Broglie wavelength of the electron (m)
radius of the nth allowed orbit (m)
number of complete wavelengths fitting the circumference

sections.tip: Write the standing-wave condition first, then substitute λ = h/mv, then show it reduces to mvr = nh/2π. Skipping the last line loses the mark that says "hence Bohr's postulate".

key_terms.definition: Model in which the positive charge is spread uniformly over the atom and the electrons are embedded in it. It cannot explain large-angle alpha scattering or line spectra.
Geiger and Marsden's 1911 experiment in which 5.5 MeV alpha-particles were fired at a thin gold foil and the scattered particles counted on a ZnS screen; it established the nuclear model.
The tiny (about 10<sup>−15</sup> to 10<sup>−14</sup> m), dense, positively charged core of the atom carrying almost all its mass.
The perpendicular distance between the initial velocity vector of the alpha-particle and the centre of the nucleus. Smaller impact parameter means larger scattering angle; b = 0 gives 180°.
The distance from the nucleus at which a head-on alpha-particle stops momentarily, where its whole kinetic energy has become electrostatic potential energy: d = 2Ze<sup>2</sup>/(4πε<sub>0</sub>K).
An allowed orbit in which the electron revolves without radiating energy, each with a definite total energy (Bohr's first postulate).
The electron's angular momentum in an allowed orbit is an integral multiple of h/2π: mvr = nh/2π.
Radius of the innermost (n = 1) orbit of hydrogen, a<sub>0</sub> = 5.29 × 10<sup>−11</sup> m. Radius of the nth orbit is n<sup>2</sup>a<sub>0</sub>.
The lowest energy state of the atom, n = 1, with energy −13.6 eV in hydrogen. Higher states are excited states.
Minimum energy needed to remove the electron from the ground state to infinity; 13.6 eV for hydrogen. The corresponding potential difference, 13.6 V, is the ionisation potential.
Energy needed to raise the atom from the ground state to an excited state; the first excitation energy of hydrogen is 10.2 eV.
Set of discrete bright lines emitted by an excited gas, each line corresponding to a transition between two energy levels; unique to each element.
The constant R = me<sup>4</sup>/(8ε<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup>h<sup>3</sup>c) = 1.097 × 10<sup>7</sup> m<sup>−1</sup> in the formula 1/λ = R(1/n<sub>f</sub><sup>2</sup> − 1/n<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup>).
All transitions ending on the same lower level: Lyman (n<sub>f</sub> = 1, UV), Balmer (2, visible), Paschen (3), Brackett (4) and Pfund (5), the last three in the infrared.
The shortest wavelength of a series, obtained when n<sub>i</sub> → ∞; λ<sub>min</sub> = n<sub>f</sub><sup>2</sup>/R.
The dimensionless ratio v<sub>1</sub>/c = e<sup>2</sup>/(2ε<sub>0</sub>hc) ≈ 1/137, which shows the electron speed in hydrogen is non-relativistic.
An orbit is allowed only if an integral number of electron wavelengths fits its circumference, 2πr = nλ; this reproduces Bohr's quantisation of angular momentum.

diagrams.title: Geiger-Marsden alpha-scattering set-up
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw the radioactive source (<sup>214</sup>Bi) in a lead cavity on the left, a narrow beam passing through a lead-brick collimator to a thin gold foil in the centre, and a movable ZnS screen with a microscope on an arc around the foil. Label source, lead bricks, gold foil (about 2.1 × 10<sup>−7</sup> m thick), ZnS screen, microscope and the scattering angle θ measured from the beam direction.

diagrams.title: Alpha-particle trajectories for different impact parameters
diagrams.how_to_draw: Put a small dot for the gold nucleus in the middle. Draw four or five parallel incoming alpha-particle paths at different perpendicular distances (impact parameters) from the line through the nucleus. The farthest path bends very little, closer ones bend more, and the head-on path (b = 0) comes in, stops and goes straight back. Mark b for one path and the scattering angle θ, and note that most paths are almost undeflected.

diagrams.title: Energy-level diagram of hydrogen with spectral series
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw horizontal lines for n = 1 (−13.6 eV) at the bottom, n = 2 (−3.4 eV), n = 3 (−1.51 eV), n = 4 (−0.85 eV), n = 5 (−0.54 eV) with decreasing spacing, and n = ∞ (0 eV) at the top; label energies on the left and n on the right. Draw downward arrows into n = 1 from n = 2, 3, 4 and label them Lyman (UV); into n = 2 from n = 3, 4, 5 labelled Balmer (visible); into n = 3 labelled Paschen (IR). Mark ionisation energy 13.6 eV from n = 1 to n = ∞.

diagrams.title: de Broglie standing wave in a Bohr orbit
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a circle for the orbit with the nucleus at its centre. Around the circle draw a wavy line that oscillates in and out of the circle and closes on itself after a whole number of wavelengths (four is a clear choice). Label the orbit radius r, one wavelength λ, and write 2πr = nλ next to it, then mvr = nh/2π. Optionally show a second sketch where the wave does not close, labelled "not allowed".

ncert_questions.q: Choose the correct alternative from the clues given at the end of each statement: (a) The size of the atom in Thomson's model is .......... the atomic size in Rutherford's model. (much greater than / no different from / much less than) (b) In the ground state of .......... electrons are in stable equilibrium, while in .......... electrons always experience a net force. (Thomson's model / Rutherford's model) (c) A classical atom based on .......... is doomed to collapse. (d) An atom has a nearly continuous mass distribution in a .......... but has a highly non-uniform mass distribution in .......... (e) The positively charged part of the atom possesses most of the mass in .......... (Rutherford's model / both the models)
ncert_questions.a:
(a) no different from. Both models give an atom of size about 10−10 m.

(b) Thomson's model; Rutherford's model. In Thomson's model the electrons sit at rest at positions where the net force vanishes; in Rutherford's model the electron always feels the Coulomb attraction of the nucleus, which is the centripetal force.

(c) Rutherford's model. The accelerated orbiting electron would radiate and spiral in.

(d) Thomson's model; Rutherford's model. In Thomson's model the positive mass fills the atom; in Rutherford's it is concentrated in the nucleus.

(e) both the models. In each, the positive part carries almost all the mass.

ncert_questions.q: Suppose you are given a chance to repeat the alpha-particle scattering experiment using a thin sheet of solid hydrogen in place of the gold foil. (Hydrogen is a solid at temperatures below 14 K.) What results do you expect?
ncert_questions.a: The hydrogen nucleus is a single proton, whose mass is about one-fourth the mass of the alpha-particle. A heavy projectile hitting a lighter target at rest cannot bounce back; it continues in nearly the same direction and pushes the target ahead. So the alpha-particles would not be scattered through large angles at all, and there would be no backward scattering. The experiment would show only small deflections and could not be used to find the size of the hydrogen nucleus. Large-angle scattering needs a target nucleus much heavier than the alpha-particle, which is why gold (mass about 50 times that of the alpha-particle) was used.

ncert_questions.q: A difference of 2.3 eV separates two energy levels in an atom. What is the frequency of radiation emitted when the atom makes a transition from the upper level to the lower level?
ncert_questions.a:
From Bohr's frequency condition, hν = ΔE.

ΔE = 2.3 eV = 2.3 × 1.6 × 10−19 J = 3.68 × 10−19 J.

ν = ΔE/h = 3.68 × 10−19/6.63 × 10−34 = 5.55 × 1014 Hz.

(Check: λ = 1240/2.3 = 539 nm, green light, and c/λ = 3 × 108/5.39 × 10−7 = 5.6 × 1014 Hz.)

ncert_questions.q: The ground state energy of hydrogen atom is −13.6 eV. What are the kinetic and potential energies of the electron in this state?
ncert_questions.a:
For an electron in a Bohr orbit, K = −E and U = 2E (since K = e2/8πε0r, U = −e2/4πε0r and E = K + U = −e2/8πε0r).

Kinetic energy K = −(−13.6) = 13.6 eV.

Potential energy U = 2 × (−13.6) = −27.2 eV.

Check: K + U = 13.6 − 27.2 = −13.6 eV = E.

ncert_questions.q: A hydrogen atom initially in the ground level absorbs a photon, which excites it to the n = 4 level. Determine the wavelength and frequency of the photon.
ncert_questions.a:
Energy absorbed ΔE = E4 − E1 = −13.6/16 − (−13.6) = −0.85 + 13.6 = 12.75 eV.

In joule: ΔE = 12.75 × 1.6 × 10−19 = 2.04 × 10−18 J.

Frequency ν = ΔE/h = 2.04 × 10−18/6.63 × 10−34 = 3.08 × 1015 Hz.

Wavelength λ = c/ν = 3 × 108/3.08 × 1015 = 9.74 × 10−8 m ≈ 97 nm (quick check: 1240/12.75 = 97.3 nm). This lies in the ultraviolet, as expected for a Lyman-series photon.

ncert_questions.q: (a) Using the Bohr's model calculate the speed of the electron in a hydrogen atom in the n = 1, 2, and 3 levels. (b) Calculate the orbital period in each of these levels.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) vn = e2/(2ε0nh) = v1/n, with v1 = (1.6 × 10−19)2/(2 × 8.85 × 10−12 × 6.63 × 10−34) = 2.56 × 10−38/1.173 × 10−44 = 2.18 × 106 m s−1.

v1 = 2.18 × 106 m s−1; v2 = 1.09 × 106 m s−1; v3 = 7.27 × 105 m s−1.

(b) Tn = 2πrn/vn with rn = n2 × 5.29 × 10−11 m and vn = v1/n, so Tn = n3T1.

T1 = 2π × 5.29 × 10−11/2.18 × 106 = 3.32 × 10−10/2.18 × 106 = 1.52 × 10−16 s (about 1.53 × 10−16 s with unrounded constants).

T2 = 8T1 = 1.22 × 10−15 s; T3 = 27T1 = 4.11 × 10−15 s.

ncert_questions.q: The radius of the innermost electron orbit of a hydrogen atom is 5.3 × 10<sup>−11</sup> m. What are the radii of the n = 2 and n = 3 orbits?
A 12.5 eV electron beam is used to bombard gaseous hydrogen at room temperature. What series of wavelengths will be emitted?
ncert_questions.a:
At room temperature the atoms are in the ground state, E1 = −13.6 eV. The energy an electron can give is at most 12.5 eV. Energy needed to reach n = 2 is 10.2 eV, to reach n = 3 is 13.6 − 1.51 = 12.09 eV, to reach n = 4 is 12.75 eV. So the atoms can be excited up to n = 3 only (12.75 eV is more than 12.5 eV).

From n = 3, three transitions are possible, giving three lines:

  • n = 3 → 1: ΔE = 12.09 eV, λ = 1240/12.09 = 102.6 nm (Lyman, second line).
  • n = 2 → 1: ΔE = 10.2 eV, λ = 1240/10.2 = 121.6 nm (Lyman, first line).
  • n = 3 → 2: ΔE = 1.89 eV, λ = 1240/1.89 = 656 nm (Balmer, first line, Hα).

So two Lyman lines and one Balmer line are emitted.

ncert_questions.q: In accordance with the Bohr's model, find the quantum number that characterises the earth's revolution around the sun in an orbit of radius 1.5 × 10<sup>11</sup> m with orbital speed 3 × 10<sup>4</sup> m/s. (Mass of earth = 6.0 × 10<sup>24</sup> kg.)
ncert_questions.a:
Bohr's quantisation: mvr = nh/2π, so n = 2πmvr/h.

mvr = 6.0 × 1024 × 3 × 104 × 1.5 × 1011 = 2.7 × 1040 kg m2 s−1.

n = 2π × 2.7 × 1040/6.63 × 10−34 = 1.696 × 1041/6.63 × 10−34 = 2.56 × 1074.

The quantum number is enormous, which shows why quantisation is invisible for macroscopic objects: neighbouring allowed orbits are so close that the motion looks continuous.

ncert_questions.q: In the Rutherford scattering experiment, the distance of closest approach for an alpha-particle of kinetic energy 7.7 MeV on a gold nucleus (Z = 79) is to be found. What does it tell us about the size of the nucleus?
ncert_questions.a:
At closest approach the kinetic energy is entirely converted to electrostatic potential energy: K = (1/4πε0) · (2e)(Ze)/d.

K = 7.7 × 106 × 1.6 × 10−19 = 1.23 × 10−12 J.

d = 2Ze2/(4πε0K) = 9 × 109 × 2 × 79 × (1.6 × 10−19)2/1.23 × 10−12 = 3.64 × 10−26/1.23 × 10−12 = 2.96 × 10−14 m ≈ 30 fm.

The gold nucleus must be smaller than this, since the alpha-particle is turned back before reaching it (the actual radius is about 6 fm). So the nucleus is roughly 104 times smaller than the atom (10−10 m).

ncert_questions.q: Using the Rydberg formula, calculate the wavelengths of the first four spectral lines in the Lyman series of the hydrogen spectrum.
ncert_questions.a:
Lyman series: 1/λ = R(1/12 − 1/n2), n = 2, 3, 4, 5, with R = 1.097 × 107 m−1.

  • n = 2: 1/λ = R × 3/4, λ = 4/(3 × 1.097 × 107) = 1.215 × 10−7 m = 121.5 nm.
  • n = 3: 1/λ = R × 8/9, λ = 9/(8 × 1.097 × 107) = 1.026 × 10−7 m = 102.6 nm.
  • n = 4: 1/λ = R × 15/16, λ = 16/(15 × 1.097 × 107) = 9.72 × 10−8 m = 97.2 nm.
  • n = 5: 1/λ = R × 24/25, λ = 25/(24 × 1.097 × 107) = 9.50 × 10−8 m = 95.0 nm.

All four are in the ultraviolet, and they get closer together as n rises, converging on the series limit 1/R = 91.2 nm.

pyq.answer: b

pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: First excited state is n = 2; E<sub>2</sub> = −13.6/4 = −3.4 eV.

pyq.q: Which series of the hydrogen spectrum lies in the visible region?
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Balmer lines (transitions ending on n = 2) run from 656 nm to 365 nm; Lyman is in the UV and the others in the IR.

pyq.q: The distance of closest approach of an alpha-particle of kinetic energy K fired head-on at a nucleus is d. If the kinetic energy is doubled, the distance of closest approach becomes
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: d = 2Ze<sup>2</sup>/(4πε<sub>0</sub>K) ∝ 1/K, so doubling K halves d.

pyq.q: The angular momentum of the electron in the third Bohr orbit of hydrogen is
pyq.answer: b

pyq.q: Hydrogen atoms are excited to the n = 4 level. The maximum number of spectral lines they can emit on returning to the ground state is
pyq.answer: c

pyq.q: The ratio of the speed of the electron in the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen to the speed of light is about
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: v<sub>1</sub> = 2.18 × 10<sup>6</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup> and v<sub>1</sub>/c = e<sup>2</sup>/(2ε<sub>0</sub>hc) ≈ 1/137, the fine-structure constant.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The total energy of the electron in a hydrogen atom is negative. Reason (R): The electron is bound to the nucleus, and energy must be supplied to free it.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: E<sub>n</sub> = −13.6/n<sup>2</sup> eV is negative precisely because the electron is bound; |E| is the energy needed to remove it.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): In the alpha-particle scattering experiment most of the alpha-particles pass through the gold foil undeflected. Reason (R): Most of the space inside the atom is empty; the positive charge and mass are concentrated in a tiny nucleus.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Only alpha-particles that pass very close to the tiny nucleus are deflected appreciably; the rest see almost no force.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Bohr's model cannot explain the spectrum of the helium atom. Reason (R): Bohr's model applies only to atoms or ions with a single electron.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Neutral helium has two electrons whose mutual repulsion the model ignores; it works for He<sup>+</sup>, which has one electron, but not for He.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The electron in a stationary orbit does not radiate energy even though it is accelerating. Reason (R): According to classical electromagnetic theory, an accelerated charge always radiates.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Both statements are true, but R is the classical result that Bohr's first postulate deliberately sets aside; it does not explain A.

pyq.q: Calculate the orbital period of the electron in the first excited state of hydrogen atom.
pyq.answer:
First excited state means n = 2. Tn = 2πrn/vn, with rn = n2r1 and vn = v1/n, so Tn = n3T1.

T1 = 2π × 5.29 × 10−11/2.18 × 106 = 1.52 × 10−16 s.

T2 = 8 × 1.52 × 10−16 = 1.22 × 10−15 s.

pyq.q: Define the distance of closest approach. An alpha-particle of kinetic energy K is bombarded on a thin gold foil. The distance of closest approach is r. What will be the distance of closest approach for an alpha-particle of double the kinetic energy?
pyq.answer:
The distance of closest approach is the minimum distance from the centre of the nucleus reached by a head-on alpha-particle, at which its whole kinetic energy has been converted into electrostatic potential energy and it momentarily comes to rest.

K = 2Ze2/(4πε0r), so r ∝ 1/K. For kinetic energy 2K the distance of closest approach becomes r/2.

pyq.q: State Bohr's postulate of the hydrogen atom that gives the relationship for the frequency of the emitted photon in a transition. Write the expression for the frequency of the radiation emitted when the electron jumps from level n<sub>i</sub> to n<sub>f</sub>.
pyq.answer:
Bohr's third postulate: when an electron makes a transition from a higher-energy stationary state to a lower one, a photon is emitted whose energy equals the difference between the energies of the two states, hν = Ei − Ef.

With En = −me4/(8n2ε02h2): ν = (me4/(8ε02h3)) (1/nf2 − 1/ni2).

pyq.q: Find the ratio of the wavelengths of the first line of the Lyman series and the first line of the Balmer series of hydrogen.
Write two important limitations of Rutherford's nuclear model of the atom.
pyq.answer:
(i) It cannot explain the stability of the atom. The orbiting electron is accelerated and by classical electromagnetic theory must radiate continuously, lose energy and spiral into the nucleus in about 10−8 s.

(ii) It cannot explain the line spectrum of atoms. As the electron spiralled inward its frequency of revolution would change continuously, so the emitted radiation would form a continuous spectrum, whereas atoms emit discrete lines.

pyq.q: The ground state energy of hydrogen atom is −13.6 eV. If an electron makes a transition from an energy level −1.51 eV to −3.4 eV, calculate the wavelength of the spectral line emitted and name the series of the hydrogen spectrum to which it belongs.
pyq.answer:
−1.51 eV is E3 (13.6/9) and −3.4 eV is E2 (13.6/4), so the transition is n = 3 → n = 2.

Energy of photon ΔE = E3 − E2 = −1.51 − (−3.4) = 1.89 eV = 1.89 × 1.6 × 10−19 = 3.02 × 10−19 J.

λ = hc/ΔE = 6.63 × 10−34 × 3 × 108/3.02 × 10−19 = 6.58 × 10−7 m ≈ 656 nm (or 1240/1.89 = 656 nm).

The transition ends on n = 2, so the line belongs to the Balmer series; it is Hα, the red line in the visible region.

pyq.q: Using de Broglie's hypothesis, explain with the help of a suitable diagram Bohr's second postulate of quantisation of energy levels in a hydrogen atom.
pyq.answer:
de Broglie proposed that the electron has a wavelength λ = h/mv. Bohr's second postulate can be explained by treating the electron in an orbit as a standing matter wave. Like a string vibrating in a loop, a wave running round the orbit survives only if it fits the circumference exactly, that is, if a whole number of wavelengths equals the circumference; otherwise it interferes destructively with itself and cannot exist.

Condition for the nth orbit: 2πrn = nλ, n = 1, 2, 3, ...

Substituting λ = h/mvn: 2πrn = nh/(mvn), so mvnrn = nh/2π.

This is Bohr's second postulate: the angular momentum of the electron is an integral multiple of h/2π. The diagram shows a circular orbit with a wave drawn around it closing on itself after n wavelengths (a closed standing wave), and, for contrast, a wave that does not close and is therefore not allowed.

pyq.q: A 12.5 eV electron beam is used to excite gaseous hydrogen at room temperature. Up to which energy level will the hydrogen atoms be excited? Calculate the wavelengths of the first member of the Lyman series and the first member of the Balmer series that are emitted.
pyq.answer:
Atoms start in the ground state (−13.6 eV). Energy to reach n = 2: 10.2 eV; n = 3: 12.09 eV; n = 4: 12.75 eV. Since 12.5 eV lies between 12.09 and 12.75 eV, the atoms are excited up to n = 3.

First Lyman line (2 → 1): ΔE = 10.2 eV; λ = 1240/10.2 = 121.6 nm. (Equivalently 1/λ = R(1 − 1/4) = 3R/4, λ = 4/(3 × 1.097 × 107) = 1.215 × 10−7 m.)

First Balmer line (3 → 2): ΔE = 1.89 eV; λ = 1240/1.89 = 656 nm. (1/λ = R(1/4 − 1/9) = 5R/36, λ = 36/(5 × 1.097 × 107) = 6.56 × 10−7 m.)

The 3 → 1 line at 102.6 nm is also emitted, but it is the second Lyman line.

pyq.q: Describe briefly the Geiger-Marsden alpha-particle scattering experiment. State the two main observations and the conclusion drawn from each.
pyq.answer:
A collimated beam of 5.5 MeV alpha-particles from a 214Bi source was directed at a thin gold foil (about 2.1 × 10−7 m). Scattered alpha-particles were detected by the flashes they produced on a ZnS screen that could be moved around the foil and viewed through a microscope, so the number scattered at each angle θ could be counted.

Observation 1: most alpha-particles passed through undeflected or with very small deflection. Conclusion: most of the atom is empty space.

Observation 2: a small fraction (about 1 in 8000) was deflected by more than 90°, a few almost straight back. Conclusion: to turn back a fast, heavy alpha-particle requires a very strong repulsive force, so the entire positive charge and nearly all the mass of the atom are concentrated in a very small region, the nucleus, of size about 10−14 m.

Together these gave Rutherford's nuclear model, with electrons revolving around the nucleus under the Coulomb force.

pyq.q: (a) State Bohr's postulates for the hydrogen atom. (b) Using these postulates, derive the expression for the radius of the nth orbit and the total energy of the electron in the nth stationary state of the hydrogen atom. Hence show that the energy is negative and explain its significance.
pyq.answer:
(a) Postulates: (i) The electron revolves around the nucleus only in certain stable, non-radiating orbits called stationary orbits, each with a definite energy. (ii) The angular momentum of the electron in a stationary orbit is an integral multiple of h/2π: mvr = nh/2π. (iii) When the electron jumps from a higher state Ei to a lower state Ef, a photon of frequency ν = (Ei − Ef)/h is emitted.

(b) Radius. Coulomb attraction provides the centripetal force: mv2/r = e2/(4πε0r2) ... (1). Quantisation: v = nh/(2πmr) ... (2). Substituting (2) in (1): m · n2h2/(4π2m2r2) · (1/r) = e2/(4πε0r2), which gives rn = n2ε0h2/(πme2). So rn ∝ n2; for n = 1, r1 = 5.29 × 10−11 m.

Energy. From (1), kinetic energy K = ½mv2 = e2/(8πε0r). Potential energy of the electron in the field of the proton: U = −e2/(4πε0r). Total energy E = K + U = −e2/(8πε0r). Substituting rn: En = −me4/(8n2ε02h2) = −13.6/n2 eV.

The energy is negative for every n because the (negative) potential energy is twice the magnitude of the kinetic energy. Significance: the electron is bound to the nucleus; to remove it to infinity (where E = 0) an energy |En| must be supplied. For the ground state this is 13.6 eV, the ionisation energy of hydrogen, which matches experiment.

pyq.q: (a) Using Bohr's theory obtain the expression for the frequency of radiation emitted when a hydrogen atom de-excites from level n<sub>i</sub> to level n<sub>f</sub>, and hence derive the Rydberg formula. (b) Draw the energy-level diagram of hydrogen showing the Lyman, Balmer and Paschen series. (c) Calculate the shortest wavelength of the Balmer series and state the region of the spectrum in which it lies.
pyq.answer:
(a) By Bohr's third postulate, hν = Ei − Ef. With En = −me4/(8n2ε02h2):

hν = (me4/(8ε02h2)) (1/nf2 − 1/ni2), so ν = (me4/(8ε02h3)) (1/nf2 − 1/ni2).

Using ν = c/λ: 1/λ = (me4/(8ε02h3c)) (1/nf2 − 1/ni2) = R(1/nf2 − 1/ni2), where R = me4/(8ε02h3c) = 1.097 × 107 m−1 is the Rydberg constant. This is the Rydberg formula; with nf = 2 it is Balmer's empirical formula, which Bohr's theory thus explains.

(b) Diagram: horizontal levels n = 1 (−13.6 eV), 2 (−3.4 eV), 3 (−1.51 eV), 4 (−0.85 eV), 5 (−0.54 eV), ∞ (0 eV) with shrinking spacing; downward arrows into n = 1 labelled Lyman (UV), into n = 2 labelled Balmer (visible), into n = 3 labelled Paschen (IR).

(c) Shortest Balmer wavelength: ni → ∞, 1/λ = R(1/4 − 0) = R/4, λ = 4/R = 4/1.097 × 107 = 3.646 × 10−7 m = 364.6 nm. This is the series limit and lies in the near ultraviolet (just below the visible range, which starts at about 400 nm).

pyq.q: (a) Draw a schematic arrangement of the Geiger-Marsden experiment. How did the scattering of alpha-particles by a thin gold foil lead to the nuclear model of the atom? (b) Explain why Rutherford's model could not account for the stability of the atom and the line spectrum. (c) How did Bohr's postulates remove these difficulties?
pyq.answer:
(a) Sketch: alpha source in lead cavity, lead collimator, gold foil, movable ZnS screen with microscope, angle θ marked. Findings: most alpha-particles went nearly straight through, so the atom is largely empty; about 1 in 8000 was scattered by more than 90°, which needs a very strong repulsive force at short range, so the positive charge and nearly all the mass sit in a tiny nucleus of size about 10−14 m, some 104 times smaller than the atom. Rutherford's calculation of the number scattered at each angle, assuming Coulomb repulsion by a point nucleus, matched the data.

(b) Stability: the electron in a circular orbit is accelerated, so by classical electrodynamics it must radiate, lose energy and spiral into the nucleus in about 10−8 s; the atom should collapse but does not. Spectrum: the spiralling electron's frequency of revolution would change continuously, giving a continuous spectrum, whereas atoms emit sharp lines.

(c) Bohr's first postulate asserts that electrons in certain stationary orbits do not radiate, which removes the collapse. The second postulate, mvr = nh/2π, selects only discrete orbits and hence discrete energies En = −13.6/n2 eV. The third postulate, hν = Ei − Ef, then allows only discrete frequencies, giving the line spectrum, and reproduces the Rydberg formula with the correct value of R.

pyq.q:
Geiger and Marsden, working under Rutherford, directed a beam of 5.5 MeV alpha-particles from a radioactive source at a gold foil about 2.1 × 10−7 m thick and counted the particles scattered at different angles with a ZnS screen. Most passed through with little deviation, about 0.14% were scattered by more than 1°, and roughly 1 in 8000 was deflected by more than 90°. From these results Rutherford concluded that the atom has a tiny massive positive core, the nucleus, about 10−14 m in size, with electrons revolving around it.
(i) Why was gold chosen for the foil?
(ii) Why are so few alpha-particles scattered through large angles?
(iii) An alpha-particle of kinetic energy 5.5 MeV approaches a gold nucleus (Z = 79) head-on. Estimate its distance of closest approach.
(iv) What is the impact parameter for an alpha-particle scattered through 180°?
pyq.answer:
(i) Gold is highly malleable, so it can be beaten into a very thin foil (so that each alpha-particle is scattered essentially once), and its nucleus is heavy, so it does not recoil and the scattering is due to the nucleus alone.

(ii) Large-angle scattering needs the alpha-particle to pass very close to the nucleus, and the nucleus occupies only about 10−12 of the volume of the atom, so very few alpha-particles have a small enough impact parameter.

(iii) d = 2Ze2/(4πε0K) with K = 5.5 × 1.6 × 10−13 = 8.8 × 10−13 J: d = 9 × 109 × 158 × 2.56 × 10−38/8.8 × 10−13 = 3.64 × 10−26/8.8 × 10−13 = 4.1 × 10−14 m ≈ 41 fm.

(iv) Zero. A 180° deflection is a head-on collision, for which the impact parameter b = 0.

pyq.q:
Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom keeps Rutherford's nucleus but allows the electron only in orbits whose angular momentum is an integral multiple of h/2π. In these stationary orbits the electron does not radiate. The energy of the nth orbit is En = −13.6/n2 eV, and a photon is emitted or absorbed only when the electron jumps between two such orbits, with hν equal to the energy difference. This explains why hydrogen emits a line spectrum and reproduces the Rydberg formula 1/λ = R(1/nf2 − 1/ni2).
(i) What is the energy of the electron in the n = 3 state, and how much energy is required to ionise the atom from this state?
(ii) A hydrogen atom in the ground state absorbs a photon of energy 12.75 eV. To which level is it excited?
(iii) Name the series to which the transition n = 5 → n = 2 belongs and state the region of the spectrum in which it lies.
(iv) Why does the spacing between successive energy levels decrease as n increases?
pyq.answer:
(i) E3 = −13.6/9 = −1.51 eV. Ionisation from n = 3 needs +1.51 eV (to bring the energy to zero).

(ii) En − E1 = 12.75 eV, so En = −13.6 + 12.75 = −0.85 eV = −13.6/16, hence n = 4.

(iii) The transition ends on n = 2, so it is a Balmer line (Hγ, 434 nm), in the visible region.

(iv) En ∝ −1/n2, so En+1 − En = 13.6(1/n2 − 1/(n+1)2) eV, which falls rapidly as n grows; the levels crowd together and merge into a continuum at E = 0.

practice_mcq.q: In the alpha-particle scattering experiment, the impact parameter for which the scattering angle is 180° is
practice_mcq.explanation: A 180° deflection is a head-on collision, which means the initial velocity line passes through the nucleus, b = 0.

practice_mcq.q: The distance of closest approach of an alpha-particle to a nucleus depends on
options: the atomic number of the target only
the kinetic energy of the alpha-particle only
both the atomic number of the target and the kinetic energy
neither; it is fixed by the nuclear radius
practice_mcq.explanation: d = 2Ze<sup>2</sup>/(4πε<sub>0</sub>K), so it is proportional to Z and inversely proportional to K.

practice_mcq.q: The longest wavelength in the Paschen series of hydrogen is nearly
Which of the following is NOT a postulate of Bohr's model?
options: Electrons revolve in certain stationary orbits without radiating
The angular momentum of the electron is an integral multiple of h/2π
A photon is emitted when the electron jumps to a lower orbit, with hν = E<sub>i</sub> − E<sub>f</sub>
The electron wave must form a standing wave around the orbit
practice_mcq.explanation: The standing-wave idea is de Broglie's later explanation of the second postulate, not one of Bohr's postulates.

practice_mcq.q: According to de Broglie's explanation, the circumference of the nth Bohr orbit equals
practice_mcq.explanation: The electron matter wave must be a standing wave on the orbit, so 2πr<sub>n</sub> = nλ.

practice_mcq.q: Bohr's model of the atom successfully explains the spectrum of
practice_mcq.explanation: It works only for one-electron systems: H, He<sup>+</sup>, Li<sup>2+</sup>. Neutral helium has two electrons.

practice_mcq.q: Hydrogen atoms in the ground state are exposed to photons of energy 12.5 eV. The atoms
options: absorb nothing, since no level matches
practice_mcq.explanation: A photon must supply exactly E<sub>n</sub> − E<sub>1</sub>: 10.2, 12.09, 12.75 eV, ... 12.5 eV matches none, so it is not absorbed. (An electron beam, unlike a photon, can give part of its energy.)

practice_mcq.q: The fraction of the incident alpha-particles scattered by more than 90° in the Geiger-Marsden experiment was about
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT quotes about 1 in 8000 deflected by more than 90° and about 0.14% by more than 1°.

practice_mcq.q: The kinetic energy of the electron in the n = 2 orbit of hydrogen is
practice_mcq.explanation: K<sub>n</sub> = −E<sub>n</sub> = 13.6/4 = 3.4 eV; kinetic energy is always positive.

common_mistakes: Using e instead of 2e for the alpha-particle charge in the closest-approach formula, or forgetting to convert MeV to joule. The answer comes out wrong by a factor of 2 or by 10<sup>13</sup>, and the examiner gives only the formula mark.

Writing the total energy as positive, or writing the kinetic energy as negative. Total energy is −13.6/n<sup>2</sup> eV, kinetic energy is +13.6/n<sup>2</sup> eV, potential energy is −27.2/n<sup>2</sup> eV. Sign errors lose the final mark every time.
Confusing the first excited state (n = 2) with the ground state (n = 1). "First excited state" means n = 2, energy −3.4 eV, ionisation energy from there 3.4 eV.
Naming a spectral series by the upper level. The series is fixed by where the transition ends: n<sub>f</sub> = 1 Lyman, 2 Balmer, 3 Paschen. A 4 → 2 transition is Balmer, not Brackett.

Taking the shortest wavelength of a series from the second line instead of from n<sub>i</sub> = ∞, and the longest from the series limit. Longest wavelength is the first line (smallest jump); shortest is the series limit.
Stating Bohr's second postulate as "energy is quantised" instead of "angular momentum is an integral multiple of h/2π". The postulate is about angular momentum; quantised energy is a consequence.
In the derivation, skipping the step that shows K = −E and U = 2E. The marking scheme gives separate marks for K, U and E; write all three, then substitute r<sub>n</sub>.
Listing only one limitation of Rutherford's model. The two standard ones are stability (radiating electron spirals in) and continuous instead of line spectrum. Give both.

Treating a 12.5 eV photon like a 12.5 eV electron beam. An electron can give any part of its energy in a collision, so it excites atoms to n = 3; a photon must match a level difference exactly, so a 12.5 eV photon is simply not absorbed.
strategy:
This is a short chapter with a small set of predictable questions, so prepare it to full marks. Budget about four hours in total.

Derive, don't memorise. Spend the first hour on the Bohr derivation until you can write it unaided in under ten minutes: centripetal force equation, quantisation condition, radius, speed, then K, U and E, then substitute to get En, then the frequency condition to get the Rydberg formula. That single chain answers the 5-mark question in every version the board sets. Also derive the distance of closest approach (two lines) and the de Broglie standing-wave argument (three lines).

Memorise a short list. The five energies −13.6, −3.4, −1.51, −0.85, −0.54 eV; a0 = 5.29 × 10−11 m; v1 = 2.18 × 106 m s−1; R = 1.097 × 107 m−1; hc = 1240 eV nm; the series names with their nf and spectral region; the n(n − 1)/2 rule; 0.14% and 1 in 8000 from the scattering experiment.

Practise the numericals. Do NCERT 12.3 to 12.9 and the 12.5 eV electron-beam problem twice each, using the 1240/λ shortcut and then checking with R. Draw the energy-level diagram with the three series from memory, and the standing-wave diagram.

Theory in point form. Prepare crisp lists for: observations and conclusions of the scattering experiment, limitations of Thomson, Rutherford and Bohr models, the three postulates, and the significance of negative energy. In the paper, a 3-marker from this chapter should take six to seven minutes and the 5-marker twelve; leave the diagram till last if time is short, but never skip labelling.
